summary:
French Polynesia is an overseas collectivity of France. French law governs matters of justice and civil status, while the territorial institutions in Papeete regulate most of daily life. A trans visitor therefore enters a legal regime in which gender recognition, detention policy and criminal-law protections are set in Paris, not Papeete.

Detention follows the gender marked on an identity document, and Article D248 of the French Code of criminal procedure requires separate men's and women's establishments. A trans woman holding a male marker is consequently held with men. BuzzFeed News, reporting in January 2018, treated this as a legal grey area rather than a settled outcome, and the arrangement governs French Polynesia's prisons as part of the French framework.

The CGLPL, France's national preventive mechanism for places of deprivation of liberty, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 on transgender persons in detention. It found that Law 2016-1547 ended the requirement of medical transition or surgery for a civil-status gender change, yet no norms were added specifying how detainees should be housed in consequence, and that serious violations persist across French detention. That treatment applies in French Polynesia's prisons.

Criminal-law protection on the basis of gender identity is national. Article 225-1 of the Penal Code was amended on 18 November 2016 to replace 'sexual identity' with 'gender identity', and since 2017 transphobia has operated as an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by imprisonment. A report of 16 May 2020 recorded a 36 per cent rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks during 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against roughly 1,380 in 2018. Hate speech remains punishable under the law of 31 December 2004, which carries up to €45,000 and/or 12 months' imprisonment.

Access to gender-affirming care locally is constrained. The government of Vice-President Eliane Tevahitua tabled a social-security Bill to fully reimburse hormonal treatment, progesterone and testosterone, on the same basis as mainland France; after heated debate in the Territorial Assembly the Bill failed to gain sufficient support. Gender-diverse care is limited by local expertise, and some trans people, known as raerae, leave for the parent country's mainland to obtain specialised services.

The national conversion-therapy ban passed the Senate on 7 December 2020 and took effect on 1 February 2022. French medical bodies have moved in the opposite direction on youth: the Académie Nationale de Médecine described the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and a 'primarily social problem'; a March 2024 report commissioned from The Little Mermaid Observatory called gender-affirming care a 'health scandal' and youth transness a 'social contagion'; and a bill banning medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, with no National Assembly action since 23 July 2024. Late-2024 guidelines from the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommend puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2.

Partner recognition follows French law: civil solidarity pacts date from 1999, same-sex marriage passed the National Assembly 329-229 on 12 February 2013 and was signed on 18 May 2013, joint adoption has remained rare since, and assisted reproduction was extended to lesbian couples from September 2021. In education, higher education institutions have been expected since March 2019 to use trans students' preferred names.

The social environment differs from the legal one. The mahu is a traditional Polynesian social role in which the holder embodies both male and female qualities and holds cultural standing, and mahu and rae-rae are visible in daily life across the 118 islands. A travel feature of 4 July 2025 described mainstream LGBTQ+ inclusivity and acceptance without Pride displays, and a visiting gay couple reported first checking whether the destination was safe. Family rejection nonetheless affects some trans people, who relocate for care and support.
tangentialFactors:
Attitudinal data suggest the overseas environment is materially more conservative than the metropolitan one: in 2014 only about 20 per cent of residents of overseas collectivities viewed homosexuality as a sexuality like any other, against 77 per cent in metropolitan France, and Mayotte reports frequent family rejection and discrimination.

The pattern of restrictive French policy formation on youth transition is national rather than territorial. A Senate bill to ban medical transition under 18 cleared the upper chamber in May 2024 without subsequent National Assembly action, while paediatric endocrinology guidance issued in late 2024 recommends puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2; the two lines of authority are not reconciled.

Historical French provisions have no stated bearing on French Polynesia in the sources available: sodomy provisions were repealed by the Penal Code of 1791 and the Penal Code of 1810 retained that silence; the indecent-exposure clause of article 330, second alinea, inserted in 1960 by the Mirguet amendment and repealed in 1980, doubled penalties where the act was homosexual, and in March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for men arrested under it with the Senate yet to vote; a Vichy law of 6 August 1942 set consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual ones, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 in 1982. Sexual orientation became a protected ground in employment and services in 1985, 'sexual identity' was added in July 2012, and 'gender identity' replaced it in November 2016.

Travel-industry framing of the territory as a relaxed gay-welcoming South Pacific culture across the 118 islands rests on hospitality and does not report any trans-specific finding for French Polynesia.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses entry, visa or border-document rules for arrivals in French Polynesia, including whether a gender marker on a passport is checked on entry or any screening that could disclose a trans status. Those questions remain unsourced here.

The encyclopaedic source used for French national legal history does not state the bearing of that history on French Polynesia. The claim that French law governs the collectivity in justice and civil status is supported by the BuzzFeed News source, but the application of individual statutes listed there to French Polynesia is not independently confirmed in the inventory.

No trans-specific violence incident, date or outcome is recorded for French Polynesia itself. The 2019 attack figures and the 36 per cent rise derive from a national report of 16 May 2020 and are not broken down by territory.

The claim about limited local expertise, family rejection and relocation rests on an encyclopaedic entry rather than a study or official record, and no figures quantify how many residents leave for care. Data on how detention policy is applied in French Polynesia's own prisons, as distinct from France's, are also unsourced.
